name: Standard Scramble (Royal Basin)
approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (2,500 ft, end of FR 2870; USFS day-use fee/permit required), start on the Upper Dungeness Trail (FST 833.2). The trail climbs gently through old-growth forest along the Dungeness River; at about 1 mile it reaches Royal Creek and the junction with the Royal Basin Trail (FST 832) — bear right/south onto FST 832 and follow Royal Creek upstream. The trail climbs gradually through forest, transitioning to open rocky, brushy terrain above roughly 4,000 ft, then reaches Royal Lake (5,100 ft) at about 6-7 miles from the trailhead (~2,500-2,600 ft gain to this point) — the last reliable, easy water and a common overnight camp for a 2-3 day itinerary. From the lake, circle to its far end and continue past Shelter Rock, a large pillow-lava overhang used as a rough bivy shelter, then through a meadow with a waterfall and along the outlet stream into Upper Royal Basin (~5,600-5,700 ft), roughly 1 more mile and 500 ft of gain — another good camp and water source (snowmelt tarns/stream, treat before drinking). From the upper basin tarn, leave the trail and climb southwest across a glacial moraine (~1 mile) to the base of a large snow (or, late-season, mud/scree) slope on the west edge of Deception's northeast face; this slope leads up toward the Deception-Martin saddle and the remnant Deception Glacier. Route-finding on the moraine and lower slope is straightforward but the rock throughout the upper mountain is loose, rotten pillow lava — helmet mandatory from here up, and watch for rockfall triggered by parties above. Above the saddle, descend/traverse about 100 ft onto the glacier remnant and work westward around Gilhooley Tower and adjoining crags (go around to the west — do not try to climb over) to reach class 2 slopes leading to the summit; the alternate line through Surprise Basin avoids the steepest ground but is long, arduous, and not recommended.

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness and Royal Basin to Gilhooley Saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,500 ft, at the end of FR 2870; a Forest Service day-use pass is needed at the trailhead. Start on the Upper Dungeness Trail (FST 833.2), which climbs gently through old growth along the river. At around a mile it reaches Royal Creek and the junction with the Royal Basin Trail (FST 832) — bear right and south onto 832 and follow Royal Creek upstream.

The trail climbs gradually through forest, opens into rocky brushy ground above about 4,000 ft, and reaches Royal Lake at 5,100 ft roughly 6-7 miles in. That is the last easy reliable water and the usual overnight on a two- or three-day trip. Royal Lake runs on an Olympic National Park quota, so an overnight needs a wilderness permit arranged in advance.

From the lake, go around to its far end past Shelter Rock — a large pillow-lava overhang used as a rough bivy shelter — then through a meadow with a waterfall and along the outlet into Upper Royal Basin at 5,600-5,700 ft, about another mile and 500 ft. Good camping and snowmelt water there.

From the upper basin tarn, leave the trail and climb southwest across a glacial moraine, roughly a mile, then up a large snow slope — mud and scree once it melts out — on the west edge of Deception's northeast face, toward the Deception-Martin (Gilhooley) saddle and the remnant Deception Glacier. Helmets from the moraine up: the rock on the whole upper mountain is loose rotten pillow basalt, and parties above you will move it.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; before July is preferred while snow still covers the loosest ground
hazards: near-constant rockfall at Gilhooley Saddle, worst at its west end - do not loiter
rotten pillow basalt throughout the upper mountain, helmets mandatory from the moraine up
steep loose scree on the west side of the upper basin
steep, exposed and serious ground - early season before July is preferred while snow covers the loosest rock
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The saddle is your fix, and it is a place to move through rather than rest — rockfall there is close to constant, and worst at its west end. Do not stop and rack up in it.

From the saddle, descend about 100 ft onto the glacier remnant and traverse west, around Gilhooley Tower and the crags beside it. Do not try to climb over the tower; go around it.

The confirmation you got around correctly is the ground itself: once you are on the slopes south of Gilhooley Tower, everything remaining to the summit is a walk on class 2 slopes. Easy ground means you are right. If instead you are on steepening rotten rock, you did not go far enough west — reverse and continue around.

One route-finding trap worth naming: the alternative line through Surprise Basin avoids the steepest ground and is described by multiple trip reports as long, arduous and not worth taking. If your line has stopped feeling steep and has started feeling endless, check which basin you are in.

waypoints.name: Upper Dungeness Trailhead
waypoints.note: FR-2870, Olympic National Forest; Royal Basin approach to Mount Deception standard route.
waypoints.directions: Drive to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead at the end of Forest Road 2870, at about 2,500 feet in Olympic National Forest. A Forest Service day-use pass is required at the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Royal Basin / Royal Lake
waypoints.directions: Follow the Upper Dungeness Trail about a mile to the junction just before the footlog over Royal Creek, turn right onto the Royal Basin Trail, and follow it up Royal Creek, through old growth and then open talus slopes, to Royal Lake at about 5,100 ft, roughly 7 miles from the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Mount Deception
waypoints.directions: Continue past Shelter Rock and Arrowhead Meadow into Upper Royal Basin at about 5,700 ft, then leave the trail and cross the moraine southwest to the snow or scree slope on the west edge of the northeast face. Climb it to the Deception-Martin saddle, drop about 100 ft onto the glacier remnant, go around the west side of Gilhooley Tower and finish on loose class 2 slopes to the summit.
